title: ReLU, dropout, batch norm, ResNets
text:
CHAPTER 16. DEEP LEARNING
SECTION 16.3. RELU, DROPOUT, BATCH NORMALIZATION AND RESNETS

AlexNet (Section 16.2) proved that large convolutional networks trained on big data with GPUs could win. Over the next few years, a set of simple techniques made networks much deeper, faster to train and more reliable: rectified linear units, careful initialization, dropout, adaptive optimizers, batch normalization and residual connections. Depth went from 8 layers (AlexNet, 2012) to 152 (ResNet, 2015) and beyond. These techniques are now so standard that they appear in almost every modern network, including the transformers behind large language models. This section explains each technique, with the math that shows why it works.

1. ReLU: a non-saturating activation

The rectified linear unit is

    ReLU(z) = max(0, z),    derivative: 1 if z > 0, 0 if z < 0

Compare the sigmoid s(z) = 1 / (1 + e^(-z)), whose derivative s(z)(1 - s(z)) is at most 0.25 and nearly zero for |z| larger than about 5. In a deep sigmoid network, backpropagated gradients are multiplied by such small factors at every layer and vanish (Section 13.1). With ReLU, active units pass gradients through unchanged.

Other benefits: ReLU is very cheap (a comparison instead of an exponential), and it produces sparse activations (many units exactly zero). Problems: units whose input is always negative output zero and receive zero gradient, so they never recover ("dying ReLU"). Variants address this: leaky ReLU, max(0.01 z, z); PReLU, with a learned slope (Kaiming He and colleagues, 2015); ELU; and smooth versions like GELU and SiLU/Swish, which are used in most transformers.

A network of ReLUs computes a piecewise linear function: the input space is divided into regions, and within each region the network is linear. The number of regions can grow exponentially with depth, one way of seeing why depth adds expressive power.

2. Initialization

Weights must start at the right scale. Consider one layer y = W x with n_in inputs, weights drawn independently with variance Var(w), and inputs with variance Var(x) and mean zero. Then each output has variance

    Var(y) = n_in * Var(w) * Var(x)

To keep variance constant from layer to layer, set Var(w) = 1 / n_in. For gradients flowing backward, the analogous condition is Var(w) = 1 / n_out. Glorot and Bengio (2010) compromised on

    Var(w) = 2 / (n_in + n_out)       (Xavier or Glorot initialization)

For ReLU, half the inputs are zeroed on average, which halves the variance, so He and colleagues ("Delving Deep into Rectifiers," February 2015) proposed

    Var(w) = 2 / n_in                 (He or Kaiming initialization)

With it, they trained 30-layer plain networks from scratch that would otherwise fail. The same paper's PReLU network reported a top-5 error of 4.94 percent on ImageNet, presented as surpassing the roughly 5.1 percent human estimate.

3. Dropout

Large networks overfit. Dropout, introduced by Hinton and colleagues in an arXiv paper of July 2012 ("Improving neural networks by preventing co-adaptation of feature detectors") and analyzed in detail by Nitish Srivastava and colleagues (Journal of Machine Learning Research, 2014), randomly removes units during training:

    training:  h_i <- h_i * m_i / (1 - p),  m_i ~ Bernoulli(1 - p)  (independently, each step)
    testing:   use all units unchanged

(This is "inverted" dropout; dividing by 1 - p during training keeps the expected activation the same, so nothing changes at test time. The original formulation instead scaled weights by 1 - p at test time.) With p = 0.5 on a layer of 4,096 units, every training step uses a different random half.

Why it helps:

  - It prevents co-adaptation: no unit can rely on a particular other unit being present, so each must learn features useful in many contexts.
  - It approximates an ensemble: a network with n droppable units contains 2^n "thinned" subnetworks sharing weights; training samples from them, and the full network at test time approximates averaging their predictions (exactly so for a single linear layer with appropriate scaling).
  - It adds noise, which acts as a regularizer, related to L2 regularization in simple models.

Dropout was essential for AlexNet's large fully connected layers. In later convolutional networks it became less important as batch normalization and data augmentation took over regularization, but it remains common in transformers.

4. Optimizers: momentum and Adam

Plain SGD (Section 13.1) struggles with ill-conditioned loss surfaces: steep in some directions, flat in others. Two improvements are now standard.

Momentum (Section 13.2; Polyak's heavy ball method from the 1960s):

    v <- beta v + g
    w <- w - eta v

with g the minibatch gradient and beta about 0.9. Consistent gradient directions accumulate, while oscillating components cancel. Nesterov momentum evaluates the gradient at the look-ahead point.

Adam (Diederik Kingma and Jimmy Ba, December 2014) keeps running averages of the gradient and of its element-wise square:

    m <- beta1 m + (1 - beta1) g                   (beta1 about 0.9)
    v <- beta2 v + (1 - beta2) g^2                 (beta2 about 0.999)
    m_hat = m / (1 - beta1^t),  v_hat = v / (1 - beta2^t)   (bias correction at step t)
    w <- w - eta * m_hat / (sqrt(v_hat) + epsilon)

Dividing by sqrt(v_hat) gives each parameter its own effective step size, large where gradients are small and consistent, small where they are large. Adam (and its variant AdamW, with decoupled weight decay, 2017-2019) is the default optimizer for transformers and most large models. Learning rate schedules, usually a short warm-up followed by gradual decay (step, cosine or linear), are used with all of these.

5. Batch normalization

Sergey Ioffe and Christian Szegedy (Google) introduced batch normalization in February 2015. For each unit (or each channel in a convolutional layer), over a minibatch of B values x_1..x_B:

    mu = (1/B) sum_i x_i
    var = (1/B) sum_i (x_i - mu)^2
    x_hat_i = (x_i - mu) / sqrt(var + epsilon)
    y_i = gamma * x_hat_i + beta              (gamma, beta learned)

Worked example: values 2, 4, 6, 8. The mean is 5, the variance is (9 + 1 + 1 + 9)/4 = 5, and the standard deviation is about 2.236, so x_hat = (-1.342, -0.447, 0.447, 1.342). With the initial values gamma = 1 and beta = 0, these are the outputs. The learned gamma and beta let the network restore any scale and offset it needs, so normalization never limits what the layer can represent.

At test time, mu and var are replaced by running averages collected during training, so predictions do not depend on the other examples in a batch.

Effects reported in the paper and widely confirmed: much higher learning rates could be used, training converged in many fewer steps (the paper reported matching its baseline Inception network's accuracy with 14 times fewer training steps), sensitivity to initialization decreased, and the noise from batch statistics acted as a regularizer, often making dropout unnecessary. The original explanation, reducing "internal covariate shift" (changes in the distribution of each layer's inputs during training), has been questioned; later analyses (for example Santurkar and colleagues, 2018) argued that batch normalization mainly makes the loss surface smoother and gradients more predictive. The method's practical value is not in doubt, but this is a good example of a technique whose success came before a clear theory.

Variants: batch normalization depends on batch size and is awkward for recurrent networks and small batches. Layer normalization (Jimmy Ba, Jamie Kiros, Hinton, July 2016) normalizes over the features of each single example instead of over the batch, and is the standard choice in transformers (Chapter 18). Group normalization and RMSNorm (normalizing by the root mean square only, without subtracting the mean) are other common variants.

6. Residual networks

Even with ReLU, good initialization and batch normalization, very deep "plain" networks showed a strange problem: a 56-layer network had higher training error than a 20-layer network on the same data. This was not overfitting, since training error itself was worse. It was an optimization difficulty, called the degradation problem: in principle the deeper network could copy the shallower one and set the extra layers to the identity, but SGD did not find such solutions.

Kaiming He, Xiangyu Zhang, Shaoqing Ren and Jian Sun (Microsoft Research Asia) solved it with residual learning ("Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition," arXiv, December 2015; CVPR 2016). Instead of asking a block of layers to learn a mapping H(x), ask it to learn the residual F(x) = H(x) - x, and add the input back through a shortcut:

    y = x + F(x)

where F is typically two or three convolutional layers with batch normalization and ReLU. If the identity is the best mapping, the block only needs to drive F toward zero, which is easy.

Why residuals help gradients. For a stack of residual blocks x_(l+1) = x_l + F_l(x_l), unrolling gives

    x_L = x_l + sum_(k=l..L-1) F_k(x_k)

and the gradient is

    dLoss/dx_l = dLoss/dx_L * ( 1 + d/dx_l sum_k F_k(x_k) )

The "1" means the gradient from the top reaches every lower layer directly, without being multiplied by a long chain of layer Jacobians. Compare the vanishing gradient product of Section 13.4: here there is always an additive path. (This analysis is from He and colleagues' follow-up, "Identity Mappings in Deep Residual Networks," March 2016.) The structure resembles the LSTM's constant error carousel, where the cell state is updated additively; Highway Networks (Rupesh Srivastava, Klaus Greff and Jürgen Schmidhuber, May 2015) had used gated shortcut connections inspired by LSTM shortly before ResNets.

Results: ResNets with 152 layers won ILSVRC 2015 classification with a top-5 error of 3.57 percent (the figure reported for the ensemble on the test set), and also won the detection and localization tasks and the COCO detection and segmentation competitions that year. Networks with over 1,000 layers were trained on smaller datasets. The ResNet paper became one of the most cited scientific papers of the twenty-first century.

Bottleneck blocks: for efficiency, deep ResNets use blocks of 1 x 1 convolution (reduce channels, for example from 256 to 64), 3 x 3 convolution (at 64 channels), and 1 x 1 convolution (restore 256 channels), keeping computation manageable.

7. How the pieces fit together, and where they went

A typical modern convolutional block (ResNet style):

    out = ReLU( x + BN(Conv(ReLU(BN(Conv(x))))) )

and a typical transformer block (Chapter 18):

    x = x + Attention(LayerNorm(x))
    x = x + MLP(LayerNorm(x))        with GELU or SiLU inside the MLP

The transformer block uses the same residual connections, normalization and smooth ReLU-like activations, trained with AdamW, warm-up and decay, sometimes with dropout. The techniques developed for image classification between 2010 and 2016 thus became the standard engineering of all deep learning.

Other important developments of the period, briefly:

  - Data augmentation and transfer learning became standard practice (Section 16.2).
  - Efficient architectures: depthwise separable convolutions (MobileNet, 2017), neural architecture search and compound scaling (EfficientNet, 2019), and the "ConvNeXt" modernization of CNNs (2022).
  - Mixed-precision training: computing in 16-bit floating point (FP16 or bfloat16) with 32-bit master weights and loss scaling, which roughly doubles speed and halves memory on hardware with tensor cores (Section 15.1).
  - Understanding generalization: Chiyuan Zhang and colleagues (2016-2017) showed that standard networks can perfectly fit randomly labeled training data, so classical capacity measures (Section 14.2) cannot explain why they generalize on real data, a puzzle that is still being studied.

8. Practical checklist for training a network

  - Normalize inputs (zero mean, unit variance per channel).
  - Use ReLU-family activations and He initialization (or the framework default).
  - Use batch normalization in CNNs, layer normalization in transformers.
  - Add residual connections for networks more than about 10-20 layers deep.
  - Start with Adam or AdamW (or SGD with momentum for CNNs), with learning rate warm-up and decay; tune the learning rate first, since it matters most.
  - Regularize with data augmentation, weight decay and, if needed, dropout; monitor validation loss for overfitting.
  - Check gradients and activations for vanishing or exploding values when training fails.

9. Summary

  - ReLU, max(0, z), avoids sigmoid saturation and makes deep networks trainable; smooth variants (GELU, SiLU) are used in transformers.
  - Initialization preserves signal variance: Xavier Var(w) = 2/(n_in + n_out) (2010); He Var(w) = 2/n_in for ReLU (2015).
  - Dropout (2012; JMLR 2014) randomly removes units during training, preventing co-adaptation and approximating an ensemble.
  - Momentum and Adam (December 2014) accelerate and stabilize SGD; AdamW is the default for large models.
  - Batch normalization (Ioffe and Szegedy, February 2015) normalizes activations per minibatch with learned scale and shift, allowing higher learning rates; layer normalization (2016) is its transformer counterpart.
  - Residual networks (He et al., December 2015) learn y = x + F(x); the identity path lets gradients flow directly, enabling 152-layer networks that won ILSVRC 2015 at about 3.6 percent top-5 error.
